**Data not available in repository.**

### Reasons for Data Gap
The NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) repository currently contains no direct partial-gravity combustion test data [F-019]. As a result, exact empirical measurements of how cabin fabric burns in lunar gravity (1/6-$g$) are not available in the repository. 

To analyze intermediate gravity regimes (such as Lunar 1/6-$g$ or Martian 3/8-$g$), researchers use experimental results from microgravity (0-$g$) and normal gravity (1-$g$) to establish physical bounding limits [F-021]. Future mission payloads—including the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) and the Lunar-$g$ Combustion Investigation (LUCI)—are slated to address this partial-gravity data gap [F-019].

---

### Related Context and Bounding Investigations

1. **Partial-Gravity Bounding and Simulations**:
   - Ground-based drop tower centrifuge tests have provided initial observations of flame spread on SIBAL fabric (a cotton-fiberglass blend) burning in simulated lunar gravity [S-025 p.2]. Computational models and preliminary tests suggest materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity compared to Earth [S-025 p.2].
   - In microgravity research, the ACME E-FIELD experiment simulated partial-gravity forces by applying electric fields to act upon naturally occurring chemi-ions within flames [F-020]. *(Note: Findings referenced from the ACME E-FIELD table row originate from an unverified LLM draft).*

2. **Anticipated Lunar Cabin Atmospheric Conditions**:
   - To reduce pre-breathe times prior to extravehicular activities (EVAs), pressurized lunar habitats and rovers are expected to operate at reduced total pressure and elevated oxygen concentrations [F-004].
   - The anticipated operational atmosphere includes an oxygen concentration of 30% or higher at a total pressure of 10.2 psi or lower [F-005]. This represents a >40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere, which substantially increases material flammability [F-006].

3. **Microgravity Fabric Flammability Research**:
   - Large-scale flame spread over spacecraft cabin fabrics (0.94 m × 0.4 m) has been studied in microgravity onboard Saffire flight tests to assess flammability limits in reduced gravity [S-021 p.2].
   - Microgravity tests (such as BASS and BASS-II) evaluate whether materials burn as well as or better in low gravity under forced flow compared to 1-$g$ upward burning tests [S-007 p.11, S-026 p.21]. In zero gravity (0-$g$), buoyancy-driven natural convection is entirely absent [F-008].

bundle.question: How would cabin fabric burn in lunar gravity?

facts.claim: Currently, NASA PSI does not contain partial-gravity combustion test data. Future investigations such as the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) are slated to address this gap.

In ACME's E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames) experiment, partial gravity was simulated by applying electric fields to act upon naturally occurring chemi-ions in flames.

Microgravity (0-g) and normal gravity (1-g) experimental results establish physical bounds that bracket expected combustion behavior at intermediate gravity levels (such as Lunar 1/6-g or Martian 3/8-g).

To reduce pre-breathe times and facilitate lunar surface extravehicular activities (EVAs), the atmosphere in lunar habitats and pressurized rovers is anticipated to have pressure and oxygen concentration intermediate between spacesuits and Earth sea-level atmosphere.
The intermediate atmosphere for lunar operations is anticipated to feature an oxygen concentration of 30% or higher, with a total pressure of 10.2 psi or lower.
According to the challenge text, this represents more than a 40% increase in oxygen concentration compared to Earth's atmosphere, substantially increasing material flammability.

In free fall, buoyancy-driven natural convection and buoyant rise of hot exhaust gases are absent, causing flames to behave dramatically differently from terrestrial flames; for example, a candle flame becomes a dim blue, spherical diffusion flame.

[General | S-025: NASA Microgravity Combustion Program Overview | Objectives]
Objectives
Edge view of Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speed (SIBAL) fabric, a cotton-fiberglass blend,
burning in air in lunar gravity (simulated in drop tower centrifuge). Edge view of Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speed (SIBAL) fabric, a cotton-fiberglass blend,
burning in air in lunar gravity (simulated in drop tower centrifuge). Left: downward burning, right: upward
burning. Conduct the first-ever observations and measurements of flame spread on the Moon. Verify whether some materials burning in partial-gravity environments may be more flammable compared
to 1g. Provide a bridge between the standard 1g material screening method
and actual behavior in reduced gravity. Candle flame in microgravity, 1/6 gravity, and Earth gravity (left to right). Candle flame in microgravity, 1/6 gravity, and Earth gravity (left to right).

[General | S-025: NASA Microgravity Combustion Program Overview | Background]
Background
FM2 is the first-ever combustion experiment to be performed on another planetary body. Building on the
success of the decades-long combustion science ground (1g) program and International Space Station
(ISS) microgravity (~0g) combustion experiment campaigns, FM2 investigates burning materials on the
Moon at its 1/6 reduced gravity level. Previous computational modeling, bolstered by experiments aboard
parabolicflight aircraft and the ISS, suggest that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in
lunar gravity compared to Earth. This means that some things that are not flammable on Earth, may be
flammable in potential habitats on the Moon and other places with reduced gravity. Since fire can be a
catastrophic hazard for spaceflight and extreme human exploration, FM2 is a critical step in determining
material flammability and safety for future missions.

[Saffire-I, Saffire-II, Saffire-III | S-021: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status | 1. INTRODUCTION]
future exploration vehicles. The current spaceflight
experiment funded and being developed by NASA
addresses two objectives. The first objective is to
understand the flame spread and growth of a fire over a
large piece of flammable material, consistent with
clothing or other fabric likely to be in a spacecraft
cabin. This sample material is approximately 0.94
meters long and 0.4 meters wide. This will be at least an
order of magnitude larger in both dimensions than any
prior low-g flame spread experiment. The second
objective is to examine the flammability limits of
materials in low gravity for comparison with results of
NASA’s terrestrial normal gravity evaluation tests. The
status of the development of the flight experiment and
the individual contributions of the topical team will be
discussed in subsequent sections.

[BASS-II | S-007: NASA/TM-20210011385 BASS-II Summary Report | 1.1 Background]
1.1 Background
BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if
not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective
using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for
flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. One objective of the BASS–II tests is to identify what is the worst case for material flammability in
spacecraft environments, and how does that compare to the terrestrial upward burning used to screen the
materials for safe use aboard spacecraft. Detailed combustion models can be validated by data obtained in the simpler flow environment in
microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to
capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability
to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems. The main variables tested were the effects of ambient O concentration, ventilation flow velocity, and fuel type, thickness, and geometry. Many of the tests focused on finding a minimum O concentration or flow velocity where a material will burn in space, to compare with the Earth-based limits.

gaps: Partial gravity: NASA PSI contains no partial-gravity combustion test data [F-019]; 0-g and 1-g results only bound intermediate gravity levels [F-021].

rules.rule: Do NOT extrapolate microgravity results directly to Lunar or Martian gravity without explicitly stating the lack of direct partial-gravity empirical data and explaining bounding logic ([F-019], [F-021]).

When queried regarding combustion in Lunar or Martian gravity, explicitly clarify that NASA PSI currently contains no partial-gravity test data [F-019]. Mention E-FIELD electric field chemi-ion simulation [F-020] and 0-g/1-g bounding methodology [F-021] if relevant.

Never assess spacecraft fire flammability solely on oxygen percentage. Always evaluate oxygen partial pressure (via calculation), total pressure, diluent inert species (N2, CO2, He), and ventilation forced flow velocity together.
If asked about rocket engine or thruster propellant fires, clearly state that propulsion systems are outside the scope of PSI microgravity science due to momentum-dominated flow regimes [F-022].

For every experimental finding reported, cite the exact test conditions: fuel type, geometry, oxygen concentration, ambient pressure, flow velocity, and hardware facility. If a condition is omitted in the source, label it as 'unspecified'; do NOT guess.
If an empirical value or data point is absent from the indexed chunks and Golden Table, state 'data not available in repository'. Never fabricate numerical values from LLM parametric memory.
When source documents report conflicting findings or values, present both sources with their respective document citations, PI names, and publication years; do not arbitrarily select one.

Clearly distinguish between empirical flight experiment findings (PSI / peer-reviewed reports), challenge guidelines, mathematical derivations, and speculative engineering hypotheses. Never present interpretation as an empirical fact.
